_comment: Final demo video (Sprint 3): one general manager's day on the offline replay of the real engine: 07:00 briefing, 09:40 order questions across several orders with the tool calls shown, 11:15 feasibility (chat, then the Feasibility page), the 'i' explanations, 14:30 chase-up with the confirmation gate, 17:00 watch, alert settings, and a question the data cannot answer. Recorded with REPLAY_STEP_PACE so the live status line is readable.

steps.say: 07:00 — before the manager asks anything, the day is already on one screen.
RED: eight orders overdue, assembly 39% below its normal range for six days, three decisions.
Each decision has one button. Nothing here was asked for: the discovery tool found it.
Every chart has an “i”. Tap it and it says what it shows, how to read it, and why it is done this way.
Why eight same weekdays? Measured on this factory: false alerts fall from 0.67 to 0.1 a month, and more weeks add little.
The 07:00 morning briefing, written on a schedule: yesterday’s output, what is at risk, what to decide today.
The full briefing: production, priorities and action items, each with its supporting records.
09:40 — on the floor. “How is the TrendCart order doing?”

type.text: How is the TrendCart order doing?

steps.say: TrendCart has six orders, so it asks instead of guessing.
Now it knows which order: ORD-005, 500 scarves, at knitting, due 20 April. While it works, one line says what it is doing.
“Show more”: every step behind the answer: the planner’s reading, each tool call with its inputs, result, source rows and time.
A second order in the same chat: ORD-120, 1,500 vests, 15 days overdue at assembly.
It remembers the conversation: “the first one” is ORD-005, not late, due 20 April. The reading is stated, so a wrong pick would be visible.
11:15 — “A customer wants 800 hoodies by the 25th. Can we take it?”

type.text: Can we take 800 hoodies by the 25th?

steps.say: It asks the one thing that changes the answer: ready at the factory, or delivered?
An estimate with its assumptions: the queue’s finish date, the on-time chance, the bottleneck. Not a yes, not a no.
Can the factory take on more orders? The Feasibility page runs the same tool over the whole queue.
Our own queue finishes 30 April, after the 25th; an eligible outside workshop could make 10 April; a smaller order does not help, the queue ahead does.
Why: the queued work plus this order is over capacity at assembly, washing and packing before the 25th.
14:30 — “That order hasn’t moved in a week. Chase it up.”

type.text: That order hasn’t moved in a week. Chase it up.

steps.say: It checks the claim first: last activity 24 March, 8 days ago, then drafts to the knitting team. Nothing is sent.
Preview first. Sending needs the manager’s exact confirmation, and it is logged. A spoken “send now” would wait for a tap too.
Only after that confirmation does it send, from the manager’s own mailbox, and the activity log records who, when and what.
17:00 — “Remind me tomorrow if packing is still behind.”

type.text: Remind me tomorrow if packing is still behind.

steps.say: A standing watch: the server checks packing against its normal range tomorrow and only speaks if it is still below.
Confirmed. And the system also speaks first: in Settings, the alert policy.
An email only for a decision needed today: a stage far outside its range, three days below it, an order that will miss. At most three a day. Off until the manager switches it on.
And when there is no answer in the data, it says so.

type.text: What revenue did the TrendCart orders bring in this quarter?

steps.say: No prices in the data, so no revenue figure. It never invents one. Every number you saw today has a source row behind it.
